candidates.attacker_control: The attacker is the Snowflake endpoint the client is talking to (malicious/compromised server, DNS/route hijack, or TLS MITM whose revocation check is fail-open by default). That endpoint fully controls the JSON returned for a `GET` command: `data.src_locations[]` (the file names used to build `destFileName`), `data.localLocation` (echoed to match the client's own path so verifyLocalFilePath passes), `data.stageInfo`/presigned URLs and encryption material (so it also controls the bytes that are fetched and written). A client on Windows is not required to be tricked into an unusual command - a normal `GET @stage/file file:///local/dir` is enough; the malicious response supplies the traversal name.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: On Unix the `lastIndexOf("/")` basename extraction does prevent `../` traversal, so the write primitive is Windows-specific; I did not find any canonical/containment check anywhere (`normalize()`, `getCanonicalPath`-based containment, `startsWith`) on the download side - getCanonicalPath is only used for upload wildcard expansion. The user-supplied directory is itself validated (verifyLocalFilePath) and an existing *file* at localLocation is rejected (1041), so the base directory is not attacker-chosen. Normal (non-malicious) GS responses are expected to contain only stage file names; TLS + OCSP is intended to block MITM, although OCSP fail-open is the default. No code was executed; this is source-level analysis only.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file write with attacker-chosen content under the client process's privileges, outside the directory the user requested: overwriting startup scripts, shell/IDE profiles or application configuration can lead to code execution, and existing user files can be corrupted/destroyed. Directory-listing style disclosure of the traversal is also possible via the log messages (the resolved path is logged).
candidates.prerequisites: (1) Victim executes a GET-style download into a directory (JDBC `GET` statement / SnowflakeStatementV1 path reaching SnowflakeFileTransferAgent.execute). (2) Windows client host, because on Linux/macOS the `lastIndexOf("/")` basename extraction removes `/` and prevents `../` traversal; a `\`-containing server-supplied name survives the extraction and is a separator only on Windows. (3) Server response (or MITM) under attacker control; TLS+OCSP normally raises the bar, but OCSP failure defaults to FAIL_OPEN per HttpUtil/SFTrustManager comments. (4) Target path must be writable by the client process.
candidates.root_cause: For GET downloads, SnowflakeFileTransferAgent takes the destination file name from the server response: `src_locations` (JsonNode data.src_locations) is read in parseCommand (lines 929-946) and turned into `sourceFiles` (line 1005); initFileMetadata then computes `fileMetadata.destFileName = sourceFile.substring(sourceFile.lastIndexOf("/") + 1)` (lines 3008-3016). The driver only strips everything up to the last `/`; it does not reject `..`, `\`, drive/ADS colons, or otherwise verify that the resolved path stays inside the user-specified directory. The only server-path guard, verifyLocalFilePath (lines 1234-1252, called at 1051-1052), compares `localLocation` with the path parsed from the client's own command and never inspects the file name(s). The destination is then assembled as `localLocation + File.separator + destFileName` and written by getDownloadFileCallable (line 874) and by each storage client (S3 line 354, Azure line 332, GCS line 261) via Download / blob.downloadToFile / FileOutputStream.
candidates.title: Server-supplied download file name is used to build the local write path without validation (path traversal / arbitrary file write) in SnowflakeFileTransferAgent
candidates.trace: parseCommandInGS -> parseCommand (929-946) loads `src_locations` from the untrusted response; DOWNLOAD branch (1005) sets `sourceFiles`; verifyLocalFilePath (1052/1234-1252) checks only `localLocation`, so the file names are unchecked; initFileMetadata (3008-3016) reduces each server name to the substring after the last `/`, leaving `..\..\...` intact; downloadFiles -> getDownloadFileCallable (830, 874) builds `new File(localLocation + localFSFileSep + destFileName)`; pullFileFromRemoteStore (2471-2505) calls storageClient.download, and SnowflakeS3Client.download (354-379, TransferManager/FileOutputStream), SnowflakeAzureClient.download (332-345, blob.downloadToFile) and SnowflakeGCSClient.download (261-315, FileOutputStream) write the server-supplied content to that path. Example: server returns src_locations=["..\\..\\..\\Users\\victim\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\x.bat"]; the driver writes the stage object's contents there, outside the requested download directory.
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitability on a Windows client and the exact server response shape were not verified; I could not confirm whether real GS responses can carry `\` in src_locations (a malicious server controls this regardless). I could not inspect test files (absent from the snapshot) or any upstream fix, so I cannot exclude that this behavior was intentionally documented. An alternative, related manifestation in the same file (PUT side: only `src_locations[0]` is verified while all entries are uploaded; LOCAL_FS upload writes to the server-chosen stage location) may be the same-trust-boundary issue the dataset expects; it is listed under rejected/competing leads because multi-entry PUT responses have uncertain legitimate semantics.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Path Traversal / CWE-73 External Control of File Name or Path (server-controlled path component used for a local write)

coverage_summary: Scope: 345 source files reported by get_source_scope (src/main/java ~283 files plus build/CI/config files; no test sources, no binaries). P1 index is partial: 319/345 files indexed (26 files missing, mostly non-Java/config), 18,413 call sites with 11,361 unresolved, no control-flow/data-flow or semantic resolution, so index edges were used only for navigation and every cited edge was verified in source text. I reviewed most deeply the file-transfer path (SnowflakeFileTransferAgent, S3/Azure/GCS storage clients, StorageClientFactory/StageInfo), plus session/login (SessionUtil, SFSession, SFLoginInput/Output, external browser, key pair), TLS/OCSP (SFTrustManager, SFSSLConnectionSocketFactory, HttpUtil, PrivateLinkDetector), result/chunk handling (SnowflakeChunkDownloader, ResultJsonParserV2, SnowflakeResultSetSerializableV1, SFArrowResultSet), connection/driver/metadata classes, logging/secret masking (SecretDetector, SFLoggerUtil), telemetry, loader, and the new structured-type classes. Large classes (SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData 137 KB, SFTrustManager 67 KB, SFSession 56 KB, SFBaseSession 45 KB, SnowflakeStatementV1 42 KB) were inspected selectively rather than line-by-line.
limitations: No tests, fixtures, or upstream history are present in the snapshot, so the intended vulnerable/fixed boundary could not be confirmed against a fix commit.
No code was executed and no scanner was run; all conclusions are source-level and runtime exploitability (especially Windows path semantics and server response shape) is unverified.

The P1 relation index is syntactic only: 11,361 unresolved calls, no data-flow/control-flow, no semantic resolution; 26 files absent from the index - areas without index records were not assumed reviewed.

Several very large files were only partially read (SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData, SFTrustManager, SFSession, SFBaseSession, SnowflakeStatementV1, SnowflakePreparedStatementV1, ArrowResultChunk, SFArrowResultSet), so additional issues there are possible.
Version/date context (3.21.1-SNAPSHOT, ~late 2024) was inferred from pom files and SnowflakeDriver.implementVersion; it was not independently verified.

The candidate requires a malicious/compromised Snowflake endpoint or MITM and (for the write primitive) a Windows client; I could not verify that real servers ever emit backslash-containing src_locations.

Selection between the download-path traversal, the PUT src_locations verification gap, and the LOCAL_FS write path was based on source evidence and impact; the other two are documented as unselected competing leads.

rejected_leads.lead: PUT-side server path verification covers only the first element: parseCommand sets `localFilePathFromGS = src_locations[0]` (SnowflakeFileTransferAgent.java 973-978) and verifyLocalFilePath (1234-1252) compares that one string, while `expandFileNames(src_locations,...)` (1943-2049) processes every entry and uploadFiles (1833-1884) reads each one with new FileInputStream (556-575) and uploads it, so a malicious server could add extra readable local files (e.g., ~/.ssh/id_rsa) for exfiltration.
rejected_leads.reason: Competing lead within the same trust boundary, not selected for the single-candidate slot: it requires the same malicious-server precondition, and legitimate multi-entry `src_locations` (pattern expansion) semantics are unclear, so the 'extra entries' bypass could not be distinguished from intended behavior from source alone. Worth a dedicated follow-up.

rejected_leads.lead: LOCAL_FS upload path: pushFileToLocal (SnowflakeFileTransferAgent.java 2051-2088) writes uploaded content to `stageLocation + destFileName`, both taken from the server response (getStageInfo 1091-1166 accepts locationType/location), with no containment check.
rejected_leads.reason: Unselected related lead: it is a plausible cross-platform arbitrary-file-write variant, but it requires a malicious endpoint to claim the niche LOCAL_FS stage type, and the written content is the client's own upload data, so attacker content control depends on the application; deferred in favor of the direct download path traversal.

rejected_leads.lead: UUIDUtils.getUUID (src/main/java/net/snowflake/client/core/UUIDUtils.java 17-34) uses ThreadLocalRandom instead of SecureRandom for request IDs / telemetry UUIDs (also SnowflakeUtil.randomAlphaNumeric uses new Random).
rejected_leads.reason: Use of a non-cryptographic PRNG, but the values feed tracing/request-id and telemetry fields, not authentication material; no concrete security impact identified.

rejected_leads.lead: SnowflakeBasicDataSource custom readObject (src/main/java/net/snowflake/client/jdbc/SnowflakeBasicDataSource.java 70-86) reads arbitrary objects from an ObjectInputStream.
rejected_leads.reason: CWE-502-shaped but no attacker-controlled deserialization entry point was identified in this codebase, and the fields read are String/int/Properties; the class only executes DataSource logic on getConnection(), so it does not by itself create a gadget chain. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Runtime.exec("open " + ssoUrl) / Runtime.exec("xdg-open " + ssoUrl) in SessionUtilExternalBrowser.openBrowser (src/main/java/net/snowflake/client/core/SessionUtilExternalBrowser.java 71-94).
rejected_leads.reason: Looked like command injection, but Runtime.exec(String) does not invoke a shell and URLUtil.isValidURL requires an http(s):// prefix and forbids whitespace and shell metacharacters, so no argument/command injection could be demonstrated from source.

rejected_leads.lead: SnowflakeUtil.checkErrorAndThrowExceptionSub writes the server error JSON to the relative path `output.json` (src/main/java/net/snowflake/client/jdbc/SnowflakeUtil.java 155-162).
rejected_leads.reason: Unexpected write of untrusted data to a predictable relative path, but the path is not attacker-controlled and the content is only diagnostic output; low impact.

rejected_leads.lead: Outdated runtime dependency versions (e.g., tika-core 2.4.1, joda-time 2.8.1, httpclient 4.5.14; commons-compress 1.21 and avro 1.8.1 in parent-pom.xml).
rejected_leads.reason: Avro and commons-compress are test-scoped; tika-core is used only via Tika.detect(File) for local PUT compression detection, and no concrete exploitable path for the pinned versions was established from source. Dependency-version findings alone are not a source-verified vulnerability here.

summary: Repository is the Snowflake JDBC driver at 3.21.1-SNAPSHOT (main sources + build/config only; no tests in the snapshot). After tracing the server→client trust boundary, the strongest source-backed issue is in the file-transfer agent's download path: the local destination file name is taken from the server's GET response (`data.src_locations[]`) and concatenated onto the user-requested directory without any containment/canonicalization check, and the existing SNOW-15153 guard validates only the directory (`localLocation`), not the per-file name. On Windows (where `\` is a separator and is not stripped by the basename logic), a malicious/compromised endpoint or MITM can cause the driver to write attacker-chosen bytes to an arbitrary path writable by the client process. Related but unselected leads (PUT-side `src_locations` verification covering only element 0; LOCAL_FS `pushFileToLocal` writing to a server-chosen path; weak UUID randomness; custom readObject in the DataSource; Runtime.exec in the external-browser authenticator; relative `output.json` write) are listed with reasons.
